relationships.description: The requirement groups one or more narrower goals as independent parts of its scope, so the goals stay meaningful on their own even if the bundling requirement is withdrawn.
relationships.evidence: A requirements document or traceability matrix lists the goal IDs as named sub-items under the requirement's entry, while each goal also has its own standalone record.

relationships.description: The parent requirement bundles child requirements as its constituent parts, and each child remains a separately trackable and verifiable statement that could be reused or regrouped elsewhere.
relationships.evidence: The requirements management tool (e.g. Jira epic/story links or a DOORS module hierarchy) shows the child requirement IDs linked under the parent, each with its own acceptance criteria.

relationships.description: The requirement and the constraint bear on the same design decision, with the constraint limiting which options can be used to satisfy the requirement, without one deriving from the other.
relationships.evidence: An architecture decision record or requirement entry cites both the requirement ID and the constraint (e.g. a mandated technology or deadline) as factors in the same decision.

relationships.description: The driver is the condition or force, such as a new regulation or rising cost, that prompted the requirement to be written and serves as its justification.
relationships.evidence: The requirement's rationale or source field names the driver, for example citing the regulation clause or cost analysis that motivated it.

relationships.description: The requirement is loosely linked to a goal it is relevant to, recording traceability without asserting that meeting the requirement achieves the goal.
relationships.evidence: A traceability matrix or requirement record lists the goal in a 'related goals' field rather than a 'realizes' or 'refines' field.

relationships.description: The outcome is the measurable end result that satisfying the requirement is expected to contribute to or be evaluated against.
relationships.evidence: The requirement specification or OKR document references the outcome's target value or KPI as the success measure linked to the requirement.

relationships.description: The stakeholder is the party whose concern the requirement expresses or who requested, owns, or must accept it.
relationships.evidence: The requirement record names the stakeholder in its requester, owner, or approver field, or meeting notes attribute the need to that stakeholder.

relationships.description: The value describes the benefit a stakeholder gains when the requirement is met, giving the stakeholder-perspective justification for the requirement.
relationships.evidence: The requirement's business case or user-story 'so that' clause states the benefit captured by the value element.

relationships.description: The requirement is a concrete, verifiable refinement of the goal, such that satisfying the requirement makes the qualitative goal achievable in practice.
relationships.evidence: A goal-to-requirement decomposition (e.g. a traceability matrix or goal model) lists the requirement as one of the refinements that together achieve the goal.

relationships.description: The source requirement is a more specific variant of the general requirement, inheriting its intent and constraints while narrowing it to a particular context, platform, or case.
relationships.evidence: The requirements catalog marks the requirement as a variant or subtype of the general one, e.g. 'REQ-AUTH-MOBILE specializes REQ-AUTH', restating its criteria with added specifics.

notes: Requirement aggregates goal inverts the usual hierarchy; goals are refined by requirements, so this should likely be removed or reversed. Requirement associated-with goal overlaps with realizes goal; prefer realizes when the requirement actually refines the goal. Aggregates requirement and specializes requirement must be distinguished as decomposition versus variant.
